* \(|E|=m\) edges, and  
* \(p\) connected components.  

Then

*Lemma.*  Every connected simple graph on \(v\) vertices contains at least \(v-1\) edges.

*Proof of Lemma.*  We proceed by induction on the number of vertices \(v\).

*Base case:* \(v=1\).  A single vertex has no edges, and \(1-1=0\); the claim holds.

*Inductive step:* Assume the lemma holds for all connected graphs with fewer than \(v\) vertices.  
Let \(C\) be a connected graph on \(v\) vertices.  Because \(C\) is connected, it possesses a **spanning tree** \(T\).  A tree on \(v\) vertices has exactly \(v-1\) edges.  Every edge of \(C\) either lies on \(T\) or is a “chord’’ outside \(T\); therefore the total number of edges in \(C\) is at least the number of edges in \(T\), i.e. at least \(v-1\). * \(v_i = |V_i|\) (its number of vertices),  
* \(e_i = |E(C_i)|\) (edges whose both ends lie in \(C_i\)).

\[
e_i \;\ge\; v_i-1\qquad\text{for every }i=1,\dots ,p .

\[

m &= \sum_{i=1}^{p} e_i 
   \;\ge\; \sum_{i=1}^{p} (v_i-1) \\
  &= \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{p} v_i\Bigr) - p

\end{aligned}
\]

\[
n-p \le m ,
\]
